newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia still waiting for government reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Russia still waiting for government reshuffle.

text.p: The Russian government, savaged by President Boris Yeltsin for its failure to cope with an economic crisis, will be extensively overhauled, but the moment of truth has been put off, Russian newspapers said on Friday.

"All the sensations everyone has been waiting for all week ...have been put off for an unknown period," liberal daily Sevodnya headlined on its front page. "Promotions, sackings and a structural reshaping of the government did not take place."
Many had expected a reshuffle in the hours after Yeltsin's state of the nation address to parliament on Thursday.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin did tell the cabinet there would be a series of significant changes in the next few days. But he named no names.
"There was no real news from Chernomyrdin," Sevodnya said. "Nothing concrete has been said about a reshuffle."
Yet Nezavisimaya Gazeta said that, despite the delay, the appointment of Anatoly Chubais, Yeltsin's chief-of-staff, as first deputy prime minister, now seemed even more likely.
"The bottom line is that the decision on moving Chubais to the government has been made," the newspaper said, noting that the liberal economist sat in on Thursday's cabinet meeting.
Kremlin sources say the liberal Chubais is to be parachuted in as Chernomyrdin's number two, taking sole responsibility as first deputy prime minister for supervising economic reforms.

Interfax news agency said on Thursday that Yeltsin, whose speech confirmed both his ability and determination to rule again after eight months of illness, could sign a decree appointing the 41-year-old Chubais on Friday.
Sevodnya was more cautious. "'Rumours were too quick to name Chubais the one and only deputy prime minister," it said, suggesting Chubais himself could be pushing the idea.
"Anatoly Borisovich (Chubais) knows how to work with the press," the newspaper said.
Chernomyrdin called Chubais, who earned the hatred of the communist opposition when he spearheaded Russia's privatisation campaign, a "high-calibre economist" who would be an asset to the government.
Yeltsin entrusted Chernomyrdin with rooting out corruption and putting the government's own house in order so as to protect free market reforms from descending into anarchy.
"Yeltsin has declared war on the bureaucracy," said Nezavisimaya, calling the speech his best in four years.
The 66-year-old president demanded an end to delays in paying pensions and wages -- a source of misery for millions.
"Enough is enough...The time has come to restore order and I will do that," Yeltsin said. But he has promised that before.
Clearly already thinking of his place in history, he reminded parliament he would step down in the year 2000.
"I want to pass on to my successor...a country whose people look to the future with confidence," he said.

It seems he may now be counting on Chubais to oblige. If he fails, then Yeltsin and the new Russian establishment that has grown around him may find themselves unable to repeat last year's feat of getting their preferred candidate re-elected.
Yeltsin was turning his attention to foreign policy on Friday.
Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko was in Moscow for talks on extending ties with his large eastern neighbour.
Promising "great decisions for Russia and Belarus", Yeltsin said deepening integration with the friendliest of the former Soviet states would be his foreign policy priority this year.
